sections.h2: Can I sell my house without an agent in Florida?
sections.html:
Yes. Florida law places no licensing requirement on an owner who sells their own home, but several written disclosures and recording rules still apply to the seller.

The paperwork falls into three groups: what the buyer must be handed before the contract is signed, what the deed must look like, and what the tax and county offices need afterward. The sections below take those in order.

sections.h2: What disclosures must a Florida for sale by owner seller give?
sections.html:
Two statutory forms apply to residential sales: a property tax disclosure summary and a flood disclosure. The buyer needs each one no later than contract signing.

Written items a Florida seller hands the buyer
ItemStatuteWhat it covers
Property tax disclosure summarys. 689.261Warns the buyer not to assume the seller's tax bill carries over, since a change of ownership or improvements can trigger reassessment
Flood disclosures. 689.302Seller's knowledge of past flooding, any flood insurance claim, and any flood assistance received

If the tax summary is not built into the contract, it must be attached, and the contract must refer to it and tell the buyer not to sign until it is read.

sections.h2: What does the flood disclosure ask?
sections.html:
It opens with a notice that homeowners' policies do not cover flood damage and that the buyer should discuss separate flood coverage with an insurance agent.

  • Any flood damage you know of while you owned the home.
  • Whether the seller filed a flood damage claim, including with the National Flood Insurance Program.
  • Whether the seller received help for flood damage, including from FEMA.

The statute defines flooding as inundation from overflowing inland or tidal water, rapid runoff from an established water source such as a ditch, or sustained standing water after rainfall.

sections.h2: How do listing rules about property taxes change in 2027?
sections.html:
From February 1, 2027, online listings must display a tax estimate and printed marketing must drop the owner's present tax figure.

Section 689.261(3) says the estimate must be built from the listing price at current millage rates, or from the countywide average rate, using data the Department of Revenue publishes. The statute adds that no one is liable for an inaccurate estimate. For a seller advertising a house, this means flyers should leave out your own tax amount, and online listings will lean on the estimator instead.

sections.h2: What goes into the deed and closing paperwork?
sections.html:
The deed is a written instrument signed before two subscribing witnesses, as s. 689.01 describes, and recording under s. 695.26 needs printed names, addresses and blank margin space for the clerk.

  • A warranty deed or another deed type that matches what you promise the buyer.
  • Printed names and post-office addresses for signers, witnesses and the preparer.
  • Stamp tax paid when the deed is recorded, at the statewide deed rate (Miami-Dade has its own schedule).
  • Clerk recording charges that depend on page count.

Because every party stays liable, the contract should say who pays. A title company or attorney can run the closing if you prefer not to handle a deed alone.

sections.h2: How does a sale affect the tax bill and my exemption?
sections.html:
Bills go to whoever owns the property of record, so the settlement statement is where a year's tax gets divided.

Paying early in November earns the biggest state-printed discount, and the discount steps down each month to 1 percent in February. Because assessment returns to just value after a sale, the buyer's bill may look nothing like yours. The buyer files a fresh homestead application. Let the property appraiser know you sold, so your own exemption is cancelled.

sections.h2: What are the tax lien risks if I skip the closing agent?
sections.html:
A sale does not erase an unpaid tax bill, so a private seller should confirm the year's taxes are paid or credited at closing.

Delinquency begins April 1, and certificates on unpaid parcels are auctioned by June 1. A certificate holder waits two years before pressing the owner, and a tax deed application may follow. For a homestead, a tax deed sale opens at the amounts due plus half the latest assessed value (ss. 197.432 and 197.502). Keep the account current through closing.

sections.h2: In what order should a private sale proceed?
sections.html:
Work backward from the closing date, since several steps can only start once an earlier one is done.

  • Order a title search and clear any liens before the house is listed.
  • Prepare the property tax summary and the flood disclosure so they can be handed over with the contract.
  • Put in the contract who bears the deed tax and recording fees.
  • Prepare the deed, then sign it before two witnesses and a notary.
  • File the signed deed at the county clerk with the stamp tax.
  • Notify the property appraiser of the sale and cancel your exemptions.

sections.h2: When are the main property tax dates a seller should know?
sections.html:
The state calendar is the same for every Florida seller.

  • January 1: the appraiser sets just value.
  • March 1: last timely day to apply for exemptions.
  • August: the TRIM notice arrives, and a value petition is due within 25 days.
  • November: tax bills are sent.
  • April 1: unpaid taxes turn delinquent.

Whatever the closing date, set the proration in the contract and ask the county tax collector for a payoff figure.

sections.h2: Should a seller order a title search?
sections.html:
Yes, early. A buyer's lender will want clear title, and a search shows liens, prior deeds and the exact names that must appear on the new deed. It also reveals whether the owner of record matches the people who will sign, which saves a rejected recording at the clerk's counter.

The search is also the moment to check for an old homestead exemption you forgot to cancel or a tax account carrying a deferral, since both affect the closing figures.

sections.h2: Can a seller still use a payment plan or deferral?
sections.html:
Possibly, though the sale changes things. A homestead tax deferral is requested on Form DR-570 by March 31 after the assessment year, and it covers taxes above 5 percent of household income. Installment prepayment must be requested by May 1 of the assessment year under s. 197.222, and partial payments are at the collector's discretion before the delinquency date.

Deferred or installment balances should be cleared out of the closing proceeds, so ask the tax collector for a written payoff before the closing date.

sections.h2: Are there other risks that FSBO sellers overlook?
sections.html:
Three come up often: lender liens, county tax liens and occupants.

  • Delinquent taxes lead down a path to a certificate sale, so settle the bill.
  • Occupants need proper notice before closing; section 83.57 sets 30 days for a month-to-month tenancy.
  • A buyer's lender will want clear title, so order a title search early.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed after a private sale?
faqs.a: Record it with the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the land sits, since the clerk records documents and collects stamp tax. Bring a deed that follows the printed-name and margin rules.

faqs.q: Is a lawyer required for a private sale?
faqs.a: No statute requires one, but a Florida attorney or title company can prepare the deed, check title and handle recording. Many sellers hire one for the closing even when they find their own buyer.

faqs.q: Must a FSBO seller give a property tax disclosure?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 689.261 requires the buyer to receive the summary at or before signing the contract. It can be part of the contract or a separate attachment.

faqs.q: Is the flood disclosure required even if my house never flooded?
faqs.a: Yes, the form still goes to the buyer, and you mark that you have no knowledge of flooding, no claim and no assistance. It is due at or before contract signing under s. 689.302.

faqs.q: May I put my present tax bill in a flyer?
faqs.a: After February 1, 2027, no. Printed marketing must leave out the owner's current ad valorem taxes, and online platforms must use estimators. The appraiser's website has an estimator.
